Warden's Board
Castellan Durn
Rook Varr
City folk say land is just land. A place to grow wheat. A place to bury your mother. A place for kings to stand.
I've dug graves in Rennfall for sixty years. I can tell you one thing for certain. The land listens.
We used to bury our dead under the floor. Grandmother beneath the hearth, uncle beneath the door.
Strangers called it grim. We called it keeping the family close. The land called it payment.
Three hundred years ago, a warlord made a promise. We bury our dead, and the land gives us harvest. And death stays below.
And it paid. Three hundred years of full barns. Kings called it their blessing. It was never theirs to give.
Then came the fever. Then came the burning crews. They said fire makes you clean. They burned everything.
And a hungry land... starts waking anyone it ever swallowed.
The first one stood up in a field near Ashcombe. Nobody screamed. That is the part people forget.
They knew his face. They stood there and said his name, and he turned around, and he answered.
Kael. Go. Now. Whatever you hear, do not come back.
That night the crown cracked. The queen died. And a kingdom needed someone to blame.
Every king wore that crown and swore that oath, and not one of them told the people what it cost.
Then it broke. And the debt came due all at once, the way debts do.
For the negligence that took Her Majesty's life, your title and your sword are forfeit. And yet, in her mercy, the Queen left you a testament.
The Vale of Rennfall. May the land treat you fairly.
They gave him a dead valley and called it an inheritance. Everyone at court had a fine laugh.
Nobody read the fourth clause. Nobody but a merchant, and merchants never laugh for free.
They sent him to the place where the dead won't sleep. They thought it was a punishment.
They forgot one thing. Whoever lights the first fire in Rennfall... holds the kingdom in their hands.
So I dug one more grave, and I waited on the road, and I hoped I would not need it.
Warden. The stone is cold and the sun is going. Light it, and let us find out what we have started.
Something out there is arranging them. The big ones carry old rank-marks under the rot. Take two, and whatever is arranging them will notice you back.
Warden's Own Notice
The Ones That Lead
The ones in plate were soldiers once. They still hold formation. Break three of them and I will believe this valley can be held.
Ser Galen
Armoured Dead
The chanting ones are not dead in the ordinary way. My office wants them counted, burned, and entered in the ledger. So do I, for different reasons.
Inspector Maren
The Ones That Whisper
They gather where the light ends and count our roofs. Put some of them down so the rest learn to count lower.
Brann Hollowell
Thin the Treeline
Nobody is asking for a house. A roof, a wall against the wind, and a place inside the light is enough to stop the crying at night.
The Refugees
Roofs for the Road-Worn
Do not look so grim. They stopped being people before I got to them. What is left is chalk, and chalk keeps the rest of you breathing.
Iskra Vell
Grind Them Fine
Rennfall iron pays better than Rennfall gossip, and I deal in both. No questions, no manifest, and a flask for your trouble.
Vesna Kell
A Quiet Shipment
Every stone we set widens the circle by a hand's breadth. It does not sound like much until the night comes.
Settlement Stores
Stone for the Hearth Ring
Walls do not build themselves, and the trees nearest the light are the safest to fell. Bring the timber in before dark.
Settlement Stores
Cut for the Palisade
The Protector requires evidence that the valley is held, not merely claimed. Survive the nights, and the ledger will say so.
Protectorate Clerk
Proof of Holding
Hold a whole night without taking a wound. I have seen two wardens manage it. Neither of them was the boasting kind.
Brann Hollowell
Not a Scratch
Still breathing. Good. Now the part nobody in the capital will teach you: what we do with the ones that fell.
As you say, Warden. Stand upwind. And don't tell me their names afterwards. I don't want them in my head.
Then I'll dig. Been waiting forty years for someone to give that order out loud.
Bury them and the ground stays sweet, and quiet. Burn them and the Marshals smiles at you. It cannot be both.
We bury them. Properly, with names.
We burn them. I will not risk the village.
Bury ours. Burn theirs. Let the Marshals count the smoke.
One more thing. A rider came at dawn, wearing the flame. She'll be at the gate by noon, and she'll want a tour.
Clever. Dangerous, but clever. The Marshals count bodies, not graves. Let us hope they never learn to count both.
A letter? Nobody writes to me. Give it here.
Brann reads it twice. Then he sits down on the edge of the well.
Tamsin Oller. Took an arrow at the ford and complained about it for a month. He farms sheep past the north ridge now. Alive, and fat.
Tell his sister that. Tell her he never learned to write, or she would have heard from him years ago.
Sit down if you're sitting, or walk on if you're walking. The fire doesn't mind either.
Forty years I've burned for this valley. The trick isn't the fire — any fool lights a fire. The trick is the earth over it, thick enough to smother, thin enough to breathe. That's the whole art.
The poachers? They'll learn. Everything that burns wrong learns, once. Then it doesn't burn at all.
You're the one who walked the pans clear. Then look here: our kiln-keeper burns by a rod, and the rod is gone — a poacher took it for a walking stick, of all the uses in the world.
I watched them lean on it down by the burn ground, arguing over whose turn to carry coal. Take it back — and if they object, remind them whose fire they're stealing.
The rod comes back today.
What's a burned stick worth to anyone?
I'll watch the ricks till you're back. Try the burn ground — they keep to where the coal is.
To a kiln-keeper? Every burn for a season. To anyone else, nothing — which is why they took it.
Don't mind me — I'm the last cart of the day. Coal for the pans, wood for the pits, and my back for the whole circuit.
Funny thing about this valley: the salt keeps the meat, the coal keeps the salt, and the trees keep the coal. Pull one out and the rest fall down. Nobody at the League thinks past the scales.
You're the warden! I saw you on the dragway. I know this whole camp — better than Wren, better than anybody.
When the poachers ran they dropped their sacks everywhere — good coal, burst and spilled all over the burn ground. I marked every spot. Rain'll mud it all away if nobody picks it up.
Show me where the sacks burst, soot-boy.
Why not pick it up yourself?
Four heaps, all inside the scorch marks. I'll tell Clod you're doing it — he'll want the credit for thinking of it.
I do! But the burn ground's Wren's and I'm not allowed past the tally line when the clamps are lit. That's the rule. You're allowed, though — you cleared the pans.
Mind the tally line. Every cord on that wagon is a notch — and right now three notches are walking around in a poacher's pocket.
When the poachers bolted from the last raid they dropped what they were carrying — including my cord-tallies. Find the three sticks in the stackyard before the League counts this camp short.
Bring them back and I'll notch you a lantern off the foreman's share — the kind that keeps its flame in wind.
Three sticks in the stackyard. I'll find them.
You count wood for a living?
Good. And don't step on the ricks — they're stacked to breathe.
Somebody has to say how much fire a valley burns. That's me. That's the tally.
Stand upwind or stand still — the burn doesn't care which. This is the Burnpits: the League's charcoal camp, where the pans' fire is made a week at a time.
Six clamps are burning and I'm short four nights of sleep. Poachers come out of the trees at dusk to crack them open — green coal, spoiled burn, my name on the shortfall.
They take cordwood too when the stacks stand dark. I can't fight them and keep the burn. You cleared the pans — clear my ground. Four of them should teach the rest.
The poachers won't strip another clamp.
And what does a cleared burn ground pay?
Then burn steady. Come back when the smoke's the only thing moving out there.
A woodman's axe and the League's thanks. We weigh here too — just in fuel instead of crust.
The pans stand clear — the count settles, and the League marks it. But a cleared pan still needs fire, and the fire is going short.
The charcoal comes from the Burnpits, a burners' camp at the valley's east edge. Wren the kiln-keeper writes that poachers strip her clamps and walk off with cordwood the pans already burned for.
Take the burners' road — it forks east off our lane, marked with a post. If the pits go dark the pans go dark, and then this whole valley is digging through ash for its salt.

Careful on the rim — a cut face does not care whether you fall or jump. I'm Brack. I ran this pit when it was still a pit: sixty souls on the face, and every block that left here carried the League's seal.

Then the pay stopped. The manifest put the blame on my wagons — said the lime money walked into a keep and never walked out. My crew held one week on credit, and then the pit went quiet. Now pit-jacks squat the cut and pick it like a bone.
The floor will stand clear. I'll see to it.
What are the jacks taking?
Then I owe you a foreman's word. Walk the lane down — and don't stand under the hoist when it creaks.
Cut blocks and the League's good name. They stamp spoil with a seal they stole and sell it as first-grade chalk. Every bag they move is a lie the valley believes.
Slab to table, table to scale, scale to ledger — that was the whole job. Now I walk the rim and the ledger walks itself.
Dess. Porter, thirty loads a day when the pit breathed. The jacks don't bother us — we carry nothing now, and a porter's hands are only worth robbing when they're full.
Tally-clerk Ines. I still post the count at this post every morning, even though there is nothing left to count — a habit the League pays better than it deserves.

The night the crew walked, three of my tally-sticks went down into the cut with them. Without those sticks the books cannot prove whose lime the jacks are selling — every sack they ship is certified by my silence.
I'll find your sticks. A count should be able to speak.
Why not just cut new sticks?
Look along the cut faces and under the slab tables — wherever a count was broken off mid-stroke.
A new stick only proves the count restarted. The old ones prove it was broken — and a League court hangs on the difference.
You're standing in my kitchen. Kettle on the fire, roof of sky, floor of chalk — best room in the valley, if you don't mind the echo.

Ket. I squatted here before the jacks came and I'll squat here after — the pit keeps the rain off better than any League roof they never paid me under. The jacks? They keep to the rim and the tables. They leave me the floor because the floor is where the pit drops its dead.
Their captain sleeps up on the hoist platform, near the stamp he doesn't dare touch. Chalk remembers, warden — and a pit remembers louder.
Mind the bench — that face is live. Cutter Rill. I stayed when the rest walked: a pit you stop cutting is just a hole, and I didn't spend twelve years learning a hole.
My kiln's cold and the League's lime bags are split all over the floor — burn-lime, good stone, going to dew. The dew will take it or the jacks will; the kiln should get there first.
I'll gather the spill. A kiln shouldn't go cold over split sacks.
Why stay when the pay stopped?
Four bags, scattered down where the faces meet the floor. Bring them back dry and I'll call it square.
Because a face remembers the hand that cut it. Leave it half-finished and it will fall on somebody — usually the somebody who least deserves it.
Seal-warden Simm. My whole office is a brass head on a wooden haft — the stamp that says a block is League chalk and not just rock someone paid for.

When the crew walked, the last clerk left the stamp on the derrick platform — on the hoist, over the deep end. I have not climbed down for it because the jacks watch that platform like it owes them money. If they learn what that stamp can certify, every bag of spoil in the valley becomes 'League first-grade.'
Then I'll go up and take it off the hoist.
What stops them from just climbing for it?
Mind the deep end. And mind what the stamp has been marking since it dropped — the jacks keep their worst near it.
Superstition. They believe the hoist hung a man once and will do it again. For once, a pit ghost works in our favour.

The pay-roll answered the manifest's last question — where the coin came from. The deserters were paid against a lime contract that the League never signed. The payments were routed through a dead pit in the hills.

The Chalkpit. The League's lime workings, abandoned mid-dig when its crew's pay never arrived — because Durn's ledgers had already spent it. A dust-white spur branches off the trade road past the salt track. The pit should be empty. If it is not, I want to know whose hands are in it.
I'll walk the chalk spur and see what the pit is keeping.

Mind the rim — a worked face does not forgive a careless step. And warden: if someone down there claims the League's stamp, they are lying. The League still has its seal. Whoever cut chalk under it is cutting for someone else.
My son drove the salt carts to Rennfall, before the valley went dark. Forty years I have watched that road for a wagon.
They say someone has lit the old fire again. If that was you, then the dead on that road are not forgotten. Tell them so.
Road dust and a Rennfall seal. You'll be the Warden, then. The Marshal's clerks said to expect you.
Keep the blade in its sheath inside these walls. Greymarch has more laws than stones, and it enforces the expensive ones.
If you are looking for the Salt League woman, she keeps to the market square. Follow the carts.
You've been talking to the Salt League woman. Good. Then you know the road is being counted.
Three wagons in ten days. No bodies on the road, which means they take the drivers too. The last was a League carter. Mira Holt.
My sergeant says they come up out of Blackthorn Hollow, past the old farm. My captain says the Hollow is not our business.
Then it's mine. Who leads them?
Not your business, or not your orders?
What happens to the drivers?
Their captain is Rook Varr. He wore a road warden's grey once. He knows how our patrols move because he used to walk them.
...Both. Someone above my captain likes the Hollow left alone. I did not say that, Warden.
Ransomed, if somebody pays. If nobody does, the Hollow is deep.
Take the trade road back toward the valley. Past the farm there is a post with its markings scraped off. Go down there in daylight, and not thinking they are farmers.
Warden! The gate let me in without a toll when I said your name. That has never once happened to me.
The League is paying me for the wagon. Half what it was worth, which from Vesna is practically an embrace.
If you ever need a carter who knows every rut between here and the valley, I'm cheap now. Very cheap.
Salt, rope, lamp oil. The League moves all of it, and the League remembers who paid.
Vesna's been asking the whole market about Rennfall for a week. Whatever she wants from you, she already priced it.
You are going back to the valley? Then you can do me a kindness that costs you nothing but a pocket.
For Brann Hollowell. My brother was in his company. If he is alive, Brann will know. If he is not, Brann will know that too.
Hear it, hear it! The Moot of Crowns is called! Every holder of a first hearth, summoned to Greymarch by the new moon!
What is a holder of a first hearth? No idea. They pay me to shout it, not to understand it.
Warden. Tobias Reed, second rider of the Ash Marshals. I am not here to fight anything. I am here to write.
Every settlement that holds a night must return a ledger of its dead. Names, dates, where they were put down. The office calls it a census of loss.
I will be honest with you, because you will find out anyway. A valley that returns a full ledger is a valley the Protectorate has measured. Measured ground gets administered.
Take the full count. Rennfall has nothing to hide.
They were people before they were entries. No ledger.
You will get a count. It will not be the true one.
You say that to my face. Either you are very new at this or you have decided I am worth the risk.
Give me your number. I will carry it. But a short ledger means a small settlement, and small settlements do not get soldiers when the trade road closes.
Thank you. I will write it clean, and I will write that the warden cooperated. That word buys you a season, maybe two.
The office pays for compliance. Do not spend it all on drink. And Warden — when the surveyors come, do not act surprised.
I thought you might say that. I have been riding four years and it is always the ones who dug the graves themselves.
I will file it as a settlement unable to produce records. That is a smaller word than refusal. It is the only kindness I can do you, and it costs me something.

Warden. The Line keeps books the way other armies keep graves — everything tallied, nothing mourned. Your inspector's report reached the count-house, and I have been sent to square the keep's account.

There is a debt outstanding — thirty silver in unpaid witness-fee for the manifest. And one question the count-house would rather I did not write down, which means I must ask it twice: where is the clerk Roane?
The clerk? Dead in the keep. I saw the body myself.
Ask the clerks' roll in Greymarch. They keep a list of the living.
Pay the fee, reckoner. The valley's books are its own.
Dead men keep the best books — nothing left to be afraid of. Then the account squares at thirty, and a name is struck in pencil. Here is your fee, Warden.

A roll of the living. They will like that phrase at the count-house — it sounds like policy. Your fee, Warden, and a word given free: whoever bought the keep's wagons will want this valley's books too.
Short answers are still answers, in my trade. Thirty silver, and I write the valley down as unhelpful but honest — the count-house reads that as a compliment.
Warden. Roane — I kept the books at the keep, before you let me walk. Your people said a man who works can stay for a meal.
I can count, haul, and I know every store worth sealing. What I cannot do is go back — not to the Line, not to Durn's kind of keeping.
Stay. The stores ledger needs a hand that knows one.
One meal, then the road. We cannot feed a deserter's shadow.
Then I am yours, warden. First rule of a good ledger: everything that comes in, twice what goes out. These were in my coat — your stores have more use for them.
Fair. More than fair. For what it is worth — the paymaster in that manifest signs left-handed. Watch for the hand, not the name.
Warden. We were the keep's watch once — the ones who walked out before Durn locked the doors. We heard the valley keeps a fire for anyone the Line wrote off.
We won't lie about what we are. We stood that wall while the paymaster's wagons turned south, and we ate their salt. We're asking for the fire's edge, not a pardon.
Bread from the watch's sack, and the fire's edge until first light.
The road south is yours. The valley isn't.
Stay. But first you tell me what the keep's stores still hold.
You feed deserters. Maybe that's the thing Durn was afraid of. We'll be smoke by morning — but the count stays, Warden. Eight went into that keep who aren't written anywhere.
South, then. For whatever it's worth — the paymaster's mark was a left hand, Warden. Watch for it on any paper that promises more than it owes.
Iron bars and salt, what's left of it — the wagons took the best of it south weeks before we walked. If you want the name of where they went, ask who paid for the road they took.
Warden of Rennfall. I carry no writ and answer to no banner, so we can both be honest: a document left the iron keep, and my employer would rather it had not.
One hundred and twenty in stamped silver for your copy of it, and your silence on the hand that signed it. Refuse, and I ride on — and nothing I said was ever said.
Silver is silver. Take the copy.
The Marshals read it first. Ride on.
Leave before my watch sees you, and tell your employer the valley keeps its books now.
A pleasure. If it helps you sleep: you were never the only copy. You were simply the only one who would have read it.
Then I was never here. For what it is worth, warden — my employer respects refusals. He budgets for them.
It keeps some of them. Yours, it seems. Good night, warden — and do look under the record house. Ledgers are only ever the top layer.
Warden. I filed your number. Nineteen dead. Then a clerk compared it against the burial stones and counted thirty-one.
I rode four days to tell you that in person instead of sending men to tell you differently. Do you understand what that cost me?
Here is what nobody in your valley knows. I have filed a short count before. Twice. Both settlements are gone now, and not because the office found out.
Why would you risk that twice?
Then file the true number. I will answer for it.
You came alone. That means you want something from me.
Keep the count short. Keep the fire high. And when someone official asks you for a list of your dead, ask yourself who taught them to want one.
No. You do not get to be brave at my expense — I already filed it short, and a correction now names me, not you. Keep your courage for the thing that reads those lists.
I want a witness who is still alive next spring. You are the first warden in three valleys who lit the fire before the Marshals arrived, not after.
Because a full count is not a record. It is a shopping list. Whoever is raising your dead reads our ledgers, and the settlements with the longest lists went first.
Don't— don't raise it. I'm warm. Touch my hand, I'm warm, I'm still warm.
Nessa Aldwin. Out of Greymarch, four days on the road with my brother. He stopped being warm this morning and I left him under a cart.
There's a cut on my arm from a fence nail. A nail. You can look at it. Please look at it before you decide.
Inside the light. Now, before the next wave turns.
Show me the arm. I decide after, not before.
You wait beyond the stones until dawn. I am sorry.
There. Rust and torn skin and nothing under it moving. Four days I've been checking it by firelight. I know what I'd be looking for.
Then you're one of ours. Get to the hearth.
What was Greymarch doing while its people walked out?
Loading carts. Not with people — with grain, and crates stamped for the trade road. They put the gate guard on the carts and the rest of us outside it.
I'll work. I can mend, I can carry, I can sit up and watch the dark so someone else sleeps. Just tell me where to put my hands.
Beyond the stones. Yes. I would have said the same in your place, and I'd have hated the sound of my own voice saying it.
Vesna Kell, Salt League, and my driver will not stop the horses, so we talk while they stamp.
One crate. Salted meat, two coils of rope, a bolt of oiled cloth, and a blade a guardsman stopped needing. Ninety coin, and I am robbing myself.
Before you ask: no manifest. The League does not route carts through plague valleys, so officially this cart is somewhere else, being somewhere else very convincingly.
Done. Unload it by the hearth.
Whose blade, Vesna? Say the name of the guardsman.
We are not buying what we cannot account for. Drive on.
I don't get names. I get crates off the trade road with the Greymarch cobbler's stamp still on the boot leather, and I do not ask why a garrison is selling its own kit.
That question was worth more to you than the crate was. Take it, and remember who let you ask it. Eighty, and the cart leaves.
Eighty. And the boot leather comes with it.
Keep the crate. I have what I came for.
Principled. In a valley this thin. Well — I will note it in my book under reasons Rennfall will be interesting to watch.
Pleasure. When the road reopens I will come back with better and charge you worse. That is what the League calls a relationship.
The leather too, then. If anybody asks where you got it, you bought it from a woman whose cart was somewhere else.
Do not raise it. If I wanted the fire out I would have let them have it on the first night.
They stand at the treeline and count your roofs because I tell them to count. Counting is not attacking. You have had four quiet nights out of me.
Look at my shoulder before you decide what I am. Go on. The rank-mark is still under the rot.
That is a warden's mark. That is Crane's mark.
I don't care what you were. You are outside the light for a reason.
Then say what you want, and say it plainly.
Warden of Rennfall, sixty-one years, and the Marshals hanged me for refusing to burn my own dead. They were thorough. They were not thorough enough.
Here is the plain version. The thing that keeps them walking is not out here in the trees. It is under your record house, and it was put there by people who signed their names to it.
I cannot go in. The light you lit sees to that. You can. Open the cellar, read what is signed, and then tell me which of us the Protectorate would rather see hanged.
Good. Keep that. You will need it when you find out who put me out here, and you find their names written in a hand you recognise.
Kestrel, Protectorate survey. My colleague holds the chain, I hold the pen, and neither of us decides anything. Remember that when you start shouting.
Your ledger reached the office. A settlement that holds nights and returns records is a settlement worth assessing. Assessment means boundary, tithe, and a name on a map.
I need the boundary walked before dusk. Where you say it runs is where I write it, and what I write is what it is for the next forty years.
Walk it honestly. The fire reaches where it reaches.
Write it wide. Include the north seam and the treeline.
Write it small. Poor ground is not worth taxing.
Honest. That is rarer than you would think and worth exactly as much as it costs you. The office likes clean figures; you will be assessed fairly and taxed fully.
Small, then. Less tithe, less notice, and no soldiers when the road closes. I have seen both choices end badly. I have never seen a third.
Bold. I will write what you walk. Understand that a wide claim is a wide obligation — every stone inside that line is yours to defend, and the office will expect you to.
That is a Greymarch binding. Where did you get it?
Ser Galen reads in silence. At the steward's mark he closes the book and hands it back without looking at you.
I have seen it. That is all I can say today. Take it back to whoever sent you, and tell them a Crown officer has seen it.
Warden. A courier came from my uncle. The letter was for me, but it was about you.
He offers me the Marrowin seat. The condition is written like a courtesy. 'Should the Warden not survive the valley.'
And what did you write back, Galen?
Take the seat. Then owe me the favour.
Ride home tonight. I will not wait for you to decide.
Nothing yet. That is the part that shames me. Three days, and I have not written a single word.
As you order, Warden. For what it is worth, I never intended to earn that seat the way he wants it earned.
The feast at Greymarch is in two days. Whatever happens there, do not drink first, and do not eat what the Duke does not.
You would use me against him. I should be offended. I find that I am mostly relieved.
Forty years I kept that stone clean and never once lit it. Didn't have the right. You do.
Now listen, because this part matters. Everything the fire touches is ours. Everything it doesn't belongs to them.
Then we make the light bigger.
Them. You mean the people buried here.
Who taught you these rules, Brann?
I knew most of them. Sold me eggs. Married my cousin. Now they stand in the treeline and wait for the light to fail.
Sleep while you can. They'll come tonight. New fire always draws them.
Aye. Every roof you raise, every wall you set, the fire reaches further. That's the whole trick of this valley.
The last warden. Before the Marshals took him for an outlaw. He wrote it all down, if the cellar hasn't eaten the book.
I'm going, I'm going. The road is safer with his crew in the dirt. See you in Greymarch, Warden.
Behind you, no, not behind. He's in the ruin by the old stones. Rook. Don't let him talk. He talks until you're close.
Cut these ropes after. If there is an after.
He's down. He's really down. Give me a moment, my hands don't work yet.
Mira Holt, Salt League, wagon forty-one. They took the salt, the mules and my driver's whistle, and I want the whistle back more than the salt.
His strongbox is under the tarp by the pillars. He wrote everything down. Rook never trusted a buyer he couldn't prove.
The strongbox is not locked. Under the coin pouches lies a ledger bound in Greymarch grey: dates, wagons, and a steward's mark beside every sale.
Vesna Kell will want that more than she wants me back. I'll walk to Greymarch. Find me there. I owe you a drink and a mule.
So the valley sends its Warden. I hoped for a Marshal. Marshals, at least, bargain.
You broke my crew for a salt carter and a few wagons. Do you know who buys what we take? No. You would not be standing there if you did.
Put the blade down, Rook. This ends either way.
Tell me who pays you, and the Marshals hear you talked.
Let the woman go and walk out of the Hollow.
It does. Yours was always going to be the short end of it.
Greymarch silver, stamped at the keep. That is all you get, and you will not live to spend it.
Walk out to where? Every road in this valley belongs to someone now. This one is mine.
Another warden up the hill. Rook's buyers sent word you might come. They did not send word you would get this far.
I was the Ash Line's quartermaster here, before the Line walked south and forgot to take the keys. Everything under this hall was mine to count. Now it is mine to keep.
The valley's food, sold back at a price. You are done counting, Durn.
Hand me the manifest and walk south after the Line.
Harrow's steward pays well. Name your price to turn on him instead.
No. I am done being counted. There is a difference, and you are about to learn it.
South is where the Line is, and a rope waits for deserters. I will take my chances with you, warden.
He pays for silence, not for swords. Whatever you offer, his answer is already in my vault — under my guard.
You came back from the keep. Show me what was worth holding a dead fortress for.
Maren reads the manifest by lamplight. Twice. At the steward's mark she closes the book and does not open it again.
Every diverted wagon received and stamped — and a paymaster's signature I will have to answer for knowing. This reaches the High Marshal tonight. Not by post. By me.
Don't — please. I only kept the books. Durn holds the dais, his men hold the corridor, and I counted what came in through the breach.
The manifest? Red chest, right here in the vault. Everything Harrow's steward sent, signed and stamped. Take it — when the Castellan is in no state to take it back.
I go at first light. The page you want in the manifest is the one with the harbormaster's seal — do not let anyone call it a forgery. The ink is too expensive to fake.
Then it is done. Durn is down, the store is yours to count. What happens to the man who kept his books?
I know every name in that book. I can read you the steward's mark backwards. Or I can walk. Your word decides which.
Walk, and keep walking south. The valley does not hang clerks.
You will answer for every line you counted. Out.
South. There is a village with a new fire — I hear they take strays. Thank you, warden. Truly.
Then the books speak without me. They do, you know. Every page of them.
Warden Voss. Inspector Maren Ashby, of the Ash Marshals. The High Marshal sends her commendation, and me.
I am to guide this settlement in the sterilisation protocols. Which begins, I am told, with a full account of your dead.
Every body we take is burned. You have my word.
We bury our dead here. That is not going to change.
Stay a week. Count what you like. Then we talk.
A week. You are not the first to buy time from the Marshals. Most of them only bought a week.
One more thing, Warden. Whatever you were sent here to die of, it is already awake in the trees. I have seen the marks.
Thank you. Truly. You have no idea how rarely that answer comes without an argument attached.
Then I must write that down exactly as you said it. I would rather write something else. Give me a reason to.

And the High Marshal sits in Greymarch in three days. My report needs your seal on it, in person. Take the east road out of the valley and keep to the cobbles. There is a Salt League woman there, Vesna Kell, who has been asking about you. See her first. She pays her debts in news.
Then I will be here until the road closes. After that, ask the Warden where I went.
Sabel Orr. I carry what the League will not: small lots, fair weight, and no manifest to sign.
Everything on the board is here on the cart. Point, pay, carry it off.
Show me what you have.
Nothing today.
Look all you like. Touching is also allowed, if you are buying.
So you're the one they sent. Knight-Captain, was it? Or is it just Kael now?
Get some rest. Tomorrow we dig. Not graves, for once. Foundations.
Alive? Me. That's the whole census. The rest are... still here, mind you. Just not the talking sort.
Hah. Clever question. Nobody told him it was worthless. They told him it was dangerous. That's why he gave it to you.
Good. Then the first thing you learn is this: light the fire before dark, keep it lit, and never bury anyone outside the ring.
Doesn't matter much out here. The land doesn't read titles. Are you staying, or are you dying? Both are honest answers.
I'm staying. Show me the hearth.
How many people are still alive here?
Who told the Protector this valley was worthless?
Heap to scale, scale to ledger, ledger to silence. Walk where you like; the flat remembers every step anyway.

Count with me. One hundred twelve loads drawn off the crust, one hundred nine entered, three sticks gone. The books cannot say whose salt walked out until the sticks are found — and a book that cannot say is a book that lies.
Each stick is split and notched twice — porter's knife on one side, mine on the other. The night crews dropped them by the pans when the salt-thieves came through. Find me three and the count closes.
Hask weighs. I count. Do not confuse them — he prices what crossed the track, I record what stayed.
Stop where you are. The count reads a load short and I intend to know whether that is a warden or a thief standing in it.
The pans. The League's brine-works for this valley: every load drawn off the crust is counted twice — once by the porter's knife, once by mine. Nothing here is free; it is only weighed.

At night the pans fill with salt-thieves — deserters who learned a sack of crust beats a sack of coin you cannot chew. They squat in the dark and carry out what the League counts in my name. I want the pans standing clear. Weigh it, warden.
The pans will stand clear. Consider it weighed.
What does the League pay for five thieves off its pans?
Then the count settles. Come back when it is short of them.
Its weight in pin and patience. The League does not haggle, warden — it balances.
Halt. Torch behind you, track behind me, and nothing crosses without a count. That's the whole law of this camp. State your business before I count you as loitering.

Since you carry a warden's stamp: Ostler — wit-warden, my partner on this watch — took the store key past the boiling row to walk it to the capital. Thieves took him coming back down. They left him breathing and kept the key. Find it before the League learns it was ever gone, and I will owe you a count of my own.
The boiling row is already on my list.
A watch owes a warden. I will hold you to it.
Good. Walk quiet up there — whatever's squatting by the store answers questions with edges.
You can hold me to it from behind the key. Bring it here and we will talk about debts.
Warm yourself. The fire is the only thing in this camp the League does not count — a courtesy from when the pans fed the valley it now charges.

I raked crust on this flat before your keep was cold iron. Then the League drove its posts and the count went down to half-measures. Watch the track at dusk — the camp fills with those the count forgot.
Careful with the cart — it is all we have left that rolls. They let us wait by the tents but not past the pan lines. Spilled salt, they say, belongs to no one. No one inside the lines, they mean.

A warden walks in and out. We do not. There are spills inside — where the rakes go wide at the crust's edge, where the heaps leak. Gather what the count will never count and carry it back to us. Four heaps' worth would feed the tents a week.
The League's rules do not feed anyone. I will gather it.
Theft is theft, hungry or not.
Spilled is spilled, warden. That is their own rule. I only argue about whose hands reach it first.
Then eat well tonight, and think of us by the tent fire. Rules fill no stomach — I checked.
The manifest named more than the keep's ghosts. Among Durn's diverted wagons is one that never reached him — a Salt League salt train, waylaid a league short of the Iron Keep.

Their works sit at the end of the salt track off the trade road — the pans, an open camp of crust and cauldrons. No walls, and this season, short of honest hands. The League asks for wardens the way it weighs: precisely, and only once.
I'll walk the salt track and see what the pans want.
Tell Factor Hask the Inspector sends her count — and remind him the valley reads a crust better than the League reads a ledger.
A die. Not the stamp — the die. The stamp marks paper; this marks the stamps themselves. Show me.
Maren turns the die in lamplight until the cut face catches the flame. Her jaw sets. She has seen this hand before — not on contraband, but in the League's own charter hall.

This was cut by a League die-sinker — the mark under the rim is his habit, not his signature. Someone inside Greymarch's charter house sold the valley's own seal to the deserters who burned it. The pay-roll's trail ends in the city, warden. In a guild hall, not a ditch.
I go to Greymarch with this tonight — quietly, and to the Marshal's ear only. When the name surfaces I will send for you. Keep the valley's fire lit; the next page of this is written in the city.
Sacks don't weigh themselves. I lift, I weigh, I mark the tally and I don't ask whose seal is on the slip — asking is how a porter ends up in the spoil.
What does the yard ship, when it's honest?
Keep your back to the wall. The watch won't stand forever.

Honest? Nothing leaves here honest. Sealed chalk goes out as first-grade lime, struck blanks go out as League pay, and the slips say whatever the die was told to say. The only true thing in the yard is the weight of what's carried.
Then I'll keep my sack-count ready. When the yard changes hands it still needs hands — ones that remember what the old ones weighed.

Don't stand on the dais edge — the boards sing and the watch hears songs. Jory. I set dies, or I did: seat the face, square the rim, strike once to prove the cut. The die up there is the only honest thing I ever made that lied for a living.

I didn't cut it — I only set it. The face came already carved, still smelling of the burnisher. But there's a second plate, the cracked one — a test strike that split and was thrown to the press line like rubbish. Whoever cut the die cut that too. The crack carries the same hand.
The crack is a fingerprint. Where did it land?
And you stayed to keep setting it?

West end of the press line, under the first bench — they built the presses over the spoil. Bring it to me and I'll swear to the cut under the Inspector's lamp. A die-sinker signs his work whether he means to or not.
Coin settles a conscience faster than it settles a debt. I take their silver and I sleep badly — same trade the whole valley's been making since the keep went dark.

Keep your voice down — the watch counts breaths, not words, but it counts them well. I'm Novak. Weigh-house clerk, League charter, third grade. They took me off the toll road three weeks past because the books here need a hand that writes true while the numbers lie.

I write their slips under watch — false grades, invented carts, a seal I didn't cut. But I keep the true count too, on slips of my own: what went in, whose name was on it, what the die pressed. Three of them are lying on the benches out there where I dropped them on purpose.
Give me the count and I'll carry it out under the watch's nose.
Why didn't you run?

Three slips: one on each press bench, close to the die's shadow. If the Inspector reads them, every name the yard was paid to hide is on the table. And warden — when the watch falls, take the pens' gate with you. I'm done being furniture.
Run where? The yard sits a climb above a pit of men who'd sell me back for a week's bread. And someone must keep the true count — a false book can't hang a man, but a true one can hang the right man.
Mind the pots — second one spits. I'm Vall. I cook for the yard because a yard that eats stays bought, and because the stew keeps me from asking whose hands stir the press.

They pay in coin that smells of the crucible — too fresh, still warm from the die. I take it, because honest coin buys the same onions. But I mark what I hear, and the pit below is just a sieve. The yard is the funnel: everything the valley loses passes through it once.
What do the die-setters talk about when the pot's loud?
Stay near the pots and out of the yard. I'll be done soon.
The die, always the die — who cut it, who guards it, who'd pay a year's wage to hold it a night. Jory set it last. Ask Jory, if you can find him sober, which is never.
Done is a kind word for it. When the yard goes quiet, the pens open and the clerks walk home — if they remember the way. There's salt stew in it for you if they do.
You're not one of the watch. They walk heavier. I'm Wicke — I carry blanks from the crucible to the press, four a trip, like bread to an oven that only bakes lies.

Last night a barrow tipped on the spoil run and the watch made me leave what spilled — said dead silver walks off on its own. Four blanks are still lying out there in the grit, west of the wall. That's a month's pay dropped in the dirt, and I want it where a month's pay belongs.
Point me at the spill and they're yours.
Why carry for them at all?
The spoil run, west run of the yard — follow the rubble piles. Four blanks, heavy as sin. When the watch goes down I'm walking the spur the way it came: down.
Because a boy who carries blanks eats. And because nobody asks a runner what the runners hear — which is everything, and none of it mine to keep.
You brought back my carter, and the man who took her is in the ground. The League owes you. That is a sentence I say perhaps once a year.
Vesna turns the ledger's pages slowly. At the steward's mark, she stops smiling.
Duke Harrow's steward. Every stolen wagon sold back into Greymarch's own stores. The Duke is starving your valley and buying its food back with the city's money.
The League can have it. For a price.
It stays with me. The Moot of Crowns will see it.
Copy it. Send one to the Marshals so nobody can bury it.
Two hundred in League silver, and the League's word that we use it well. A pleasure.
Then guard it better than Rook did. Men who sell a valley's food will not stop at a book.
Two copies, two sealed letters. Careful. I am starting to like you, which is bad for business.
One more thing. The last page: deliveries to the old iron keep north of the city, every week, under guard. Whatever Harrow is building, he is building it there.
Vesna Kell, Salt League. I sell salt, rope, iron, and information. Today the information is free, which should worry you.
Your testament has a fourth clause. Whoever lights the first hearth in Rennfall may call the Moot of Crowns.
You already lit it. So the question is no longer whether you matter. It is who buys you first.
Name your price for the road contract.
Rennfall is not for sale. Not to anyone.
Who else have you told?
Twelve percent of everything that leaves the valley, and the League keeps your road open. Bandits included.
Either way: men in unmarked boots have been counting your wagons for three days. That part I am giving you for nothing.
Admirable. Expensive, but admirable. When the first wagon burns, my offer will still be here, at a worse rate.
Honestly? Duke Harrow, yesterday. I would have told you first, but you had no money yesterday.
I dig the graves now Brann's hands have gone. Twelve since the road, and not one of them stayed put.
Don't look at me like that. Somebody has to know where everyone is buried, or we bury them twice.
Cooper by trade. Forty barrels a season in Greymarch, and here I am hooping buckets for a village with one well.
Do not pity me. A man with a trade eats. A man who can seal a barrel against rain eats twice.
Winna's pot? It cracked because she boils it dry. Tell her I said so.
Here. Iron, not clay. Bring it back with a bowl in it and we will call it even.
Everyone walks a little wider around my table. That is fine. They still come when a wound goes green.
Bring me bone dust and I will make something that keeps a man breathing through a night. Do not ask whose bone.
Are you the Warden? Mam says a Warden is just someone who didn't leave.
I keep the lamps filled. All of them, every evening, even the one by the ruin nobody goes near.
I wove the cloth they wrapped half this village in. Now I weave for the living again, and my hands do not know the difference.
Light it every night, Warden. Not because of what is out there. Because of what we become on the nights we do not.
Bryd — I keep the mill's count. Every stook that leaves this hill is notched twice: once on my stick, once on the carter's. That's how the League knows whose flour it weighs.
Three of my tally-sticks went down in the field when the raiders came through — dropped between the rows where the count broke. Without them the books say the mill ground grain that doesn't exist.
Walk the stook rows and pick them up. A stick under your hand counts better than a guess in my book.
I'll find your three sticks.
Why not just cut new ones?
Good. The notches remember what the men forgot.
A fresh stick holds no memory of the load it counted — the League counts only what was notched when the grain stood. Find the old ones.
Mind the vanes — they don't stop for a visitor, they stop for no wind. I'm Corl; this is the Windrest, the knoll that grinds for Rennfall and the League's count both.

But the vanes are turning over a field I can't work. Grain-raiders — deserters mostly — squat the stook rows at dusk and carry off sheaves by the armload. My cart stands loaded and doesn't dare the lane.
You've cleared the League's ground before, the count's man tells it. Clear my field — four of them off it and the rest will remember the hill has a master.
The field will stand clear by nightfall.
What does a cleared field pay a Warden?
Then work the rows while I work the stones. Come back when the field's quiet again.
An oak shield off the League's stores and the mill's thanks — the shield's the better half of that bargain, mind.
Odle — I pull the mill's cart, when a cart is allowed to roll. For now I walk the lane so the ruts remember wheels and the raiders remember someone still claims it.
Odo — the League's count sits where the sacks are weighed, which is here, under this canopy, not up at the manor where it's warmer. Stand clear of the scale.
The mill's count runs through Bryd's sticks and my book, and until the field clears, both of us count what we already know: nothing is moving down the hill.
I'm Tam — I stack the meal and load the cart, or I did before the raiders made the lane a dice game. The cart's half-loaded and hasn't rolled in days.

Last time Odle tried the lane they cut the cart rope and let the sacks fall where they would — four of them, spilled white down the hill. It's the League's flour, and I'll take the blame for every spilt sack.
If you're walking down anyway, pick them up where they split — you'll see the white against the grass. Four sacks and the count comes back even.
I'll carry the four sacks back.
What's a sack of meal worth to a boy?
Mind the grass off the lane — they spill where they fall, and some fell far.
A lamp of lamp oil and my name off the tally — the oil's worth more, but the name's worth everything.
You've steadied the hearth, so I'll ask after my pot. My meal barrel's near the dust — the Windrest mill hasn't sent a cart down the north lane in a fortnight.
The knoll's past the north gate where the street lets out. Miller Corl grinds for the League and the town alike — if his vanes have stopped, something's squatting on his hill.
Walk up and see. A cook with no flour is just a woman staring at a cold pot, and I refuse to be her.
The road has closed behind you.
A Marshal's rider has come up the valley road.
A clerk in Line grey unslings a lacquered box of tallies at the village edge.
It was not left unwatched.
Wood-poachers strip the clamps.
The rod's 'borrowers' object.
Go and speak to them

Somebody's lucky tooth. Luckier for them that it is not still in their mouth.
Tooth on a Cord
Made for a lord who never came back for it.
Sunfire Amulet
The enlistment coin of a dead kingdom, drilled and hung on cord. Wear it and a dead payroll remembers you kindly.
The King's Shilling
Blue as meltwater. It steadies the breath in a long fight.
Riverstone Pendant
Issued to the crews who walk into burning villages. It smells of smoke and will not stop.
Ash Marshal Harness
Iskra's work: splints of femur bound in grave wax. The dead hesitate before striking their own.
Bone Lattice
Half armour, half apron — leather a thumb thick, scorched at the hem. You are slower. Nothing else that hits you notices.
Forgemaster's Apron
The lion was scratched off the breast. Kael did that himself, on the road.
Crown Guard Mail
A weigh-yard officer's mail — the scales stamped on each link so no one forgets what it protects.
League Half-Mail
Refugee stitching over a soldier's cut. Warm, which counts for more out here.
Padded Coat
Someone's winter coat, cut down twice and handed on twice more.
Patched Wool
Waxed against rain and grave-damp, with deep pockets for what wardens are not supposed to carry.
Warden's Long Coat
Taken from the drowned waystation. Still smells faintly of wet ash.
Warden's Plate
Meant for roots, not bone. It stopped caring about the difference two winters ago.
Gravecutter
Ducal issue. Heavy enough that the Duke's men swing it with both hands and their whole grudge.
Greymarch Warcleaver
Heavy, slow, honest. Splits pine and bone with equal patience.
Woodcutter's Axe
Boiled, dried, rolled. The only medicine in the valley that never runs out.
Boiled Linen
Every step rings like a small bell. Stealth is for other people.
Knight's Sabatons
Heavier than they look, lighter than they sound.
Plated Boots
Resoled twice. Still let in the rain on the left.
Road Boots
Tobias made it from a yew that grew out of a mass grave. He will tell you that story only once.
Blackfletch
Drawn properly it puts a shaft through a skull at eighty paces. Drawn badly it breaks your thumb.
Longbow of the Vale
Tobias carved the nocks himself. Illegal on three counts, useful on all of them.
Poacher's Bow
Plain self-bow of yew heartwood — drawn flat, shot flat, aimed for the hollow of a throat.
Yew Flatbow
A stamped-offhand blade from the die yard — struck, not forged, and sharper for it. The coiners' idea of small change.
The Flicker
A merchant's knife, balanced for throwing and for deniability.
Quiet Work
Two days old at best. In Rennfall, that makes it fresh.
Hard Ration Bread
League-cured and League-priced. Chews like rope, keeps a watchman upright until dawn.
Salt Meat
Root vegetables, salt pork, and whatever the traps caught. Eaten standing, always.
Hearth Stew
Gold on the cuffs so the men could see which hand gave the order.
Captain's Gauntlets
Plates over the knuckles, leather in the palm. The dead do not like being punched with them.
Iron-backed Gauntlets
Stiff with old sap. They grip an axe handle like they were made for it.
Work Gloves
A T-faced helm found in a pan-house where no soldier should have stood so long. Its last wearer held. The helm remembers.
Barbute of the Stand
Keeps the rain out. Does nothing about what walks in it.
Oiled Hood
A brimmed iron hat honest as a soup pot. Keeps the rain off; keeps a little of the sword off too.
Kettle Helm
Filtered cloth and smoked glass. You can breathe in a burning street, and be told apart from the people in it.
Soot Hood
The dent is from a mace at the palace. The owner survived. Barely.
Dented Sallet
Keeps rain off the neck and lets everyone see your face. Brann says the second part matters more.
Warden's Wide Hat
Parade armour that turned out to be real armour.
Gilded Greaves
Cold in the morning, warm by noon, heavy by evening.
Mail Leggings
Patched at the knee. Every warden kneels more than they admit.
Leather Breeches
Iron-headed and ledger-long — the mace the toll house issued before the tolls stopped being honest. It settles arguments the way ledgers never could.
Tollkeeper's Mace
Ground from the restless dead. The Marshals calls owning it a crime. Iskra calls it Tuesday.
Bone Dust
Sheds rain off a roof or off a wound. The settlement never has enough of either use.
Oiled Cloth
Scraped from coffins that were never opened. Seals oaths and wounds alike.
Grave Wax
Deer, mostly. The valley's deer have been nervous for forty years.
Cured Hide
Dark, dense, and the reason Duke Harrow keeps sending 'bandits'.
Rennfall Iron
Hand-forged, uneven, and worth more than the plank they hold.
Iron Nails
Waterproofs a roof, seals a wound badly, and burns like a promise.
Pine Pitch
Holds roofs down, holds prisoners still, holds a bridge together for one more crossing.
Tarred Rope
League currency in all but name. Preserves meat, pays bribes, melts in rain.
Salt Brick
Hearths, foundations, and grave markers. Mostly grave markers, lately.
Quarried Stone
Cut from the black pines. Every wall in the village starts here.
Seasoned Timber
Throw it, light it, and do not stand downwind of your own idea.
Pitch Flask
Brewed for soldiers who must keep standing. Three of these and you will feel nothing at all.
Surgeon's Flask
Iskra distills it from hearth ash. It burns all the way down and the burn is the point.
Emberwine
The dark goes grey and the cold goes sharp. Do not use it twice in one night.
Nightsight Tincture
Tastes like a wet cellar. Closes wounds anyway.
Bitterroot Draught
Tastes of wet slate. For an hour, a blade feels like a shove.
Stoneskin Draught
Every village cleared, with a column for souls accounted. The last column is always full and always wrong.
Burning Crew Ledger
Coal that rang like a pot when it broke — the good kind, worth the picking before rain turns it back to mud.
Heaped Clean Coal
A split stick notched by the foreman's knife — one cord of burnwood, owed and counted. Until it is back on the tally post the stackyard reads short.
Dropped Cord-Tally
Forty years of burials, listed by name. The last entry is not a name. It is an apology.
Warden Crane's Journal
Boots, arrows and salt pork, issued to men who are officially bandits.
Greymarch Supply Ledger
Every diverted wagon received at the iron keep, stamped with a harbormaster's seal and a paymaster's left-handed mark.
The Keep's Manifest
A scorched ash-rod, ringed where a clamp should stand and notched where the earth should lie over it. Without it a kiln-keeper burns by guess.
The Keeper's Measuring Rod
Stamped twice and signed once. It says Rennfall cooperates, which is a shield until it is a receipt.
Writ of Compliance
A slashed sack of Windrest flour, split open where the cart rope was cut. Heavy with grass seeds now, but it was the League's count when it fell.
Spilled Meal Sack
A split hazel stick notched twice — Bryd's knife and the carter's. Every notch is a stook of grain the League's book still believes in.
The Mill's Tally-Stick
Signed, sealed, and worth a war. Holding it makes you the most invited and most hunted person in Valcaris.
Writ of the Moot
Sealed with candle wax and addressed, in careful capitals, to Brann Hollowell.
Oona's Letter
'Should the Hearth Right prove valid, the valley is to be cleared by fire. No exceptions are granted.'
Sealed Writ of the Ash Marshals
A roll of pay-chits marked in a hand that is not Ash Line issue, each stamped with the same left-handed sign.
The Deserters' Pay-Roll
A burst sack of burn-lime, gathered off the pit floor before the dew takes it. Worth little to a thief and everything to a kiln that has gone cold.
Split Lime Bag
Brass-headed, chalk-flecked — the stamp that made a cut block League property and a cart-load legal. The last clerk left it on the hoist and never came back for it.
The Pit's Seal-Stamp
A chalk-stained stick split for the count — cut face, cart, and kiln each holding a third of the truth. Where it lies is where a load of lime stopped being anybody's.
Dropped Tally-Stick
A clerk's tally-book, its spine cracked from being thrown. The pages still add up to every bar of iron the keep ever held.
Roane's Tally-Book
Salt the scale never counted, gathered handful by handful off the crust. The League's rule says it belongs to no one; the gleaners' rule says it belongs to the hungry.
Spilled Salt, Gathered
A split stick notched by two knives — the porter's count and the pan-keeper's. Where it lies is where a load of crust stopped being counted.
Dropped Tally-Stick
A bright disc of unstruck silver, dropped where a barrow tipped. Worth a month's wage before it ever becomes a lie.
Silver Blank
A steel stamp-block still dark with ink — the face that strikes every false seal the valley has swallowed. Under the rim, a die-sinker's habit mark no court would mistake.
The Master Die
A test strike that split under the hammer and was thrown to the spoil — but the crack holds the same hand that cut the master die. Evidence that leaks like light.
Cracked Die-Plate

Standard issue, notched from a night you do not talk about. They let you keep it. That was the mercy.

Shuttered on three sides. You see the road; the road does not see you.

Brann's spare. Carrying it marks you as someone who intends to bury people properly.

Fire keeps the cold out, the dark back, and the dead honest.

Two coins wired together, carried four days out of Greymarch by someone who arrived and someone who did not.
